contributions: RADAR, a routing framework that treats configuration selection as a psychometric measurement problem rather than a learned black-box mapping.

A custom item response theory model fitted to the matrix of responses from each {model, budget} configuration across a calibration set of queries, jointly estimating a latent difficulty per query and a latent ability per configuration — both interpretable by construction.
A routing rule that follows directly from those parameters: match query difficulty to configuration ability.

Out-of-distribution generalization: the difficulty parameter is made predictable for unseen queries, so routing extends beyond the calibration set, tested on all eight benchmarks including long-context document QA.
Scalability to new models: a new configuration's ability is estimated by dynamically selecting a small set of evaluation queries, so integrating a model does not require full re-evaluation.
limitations: No standalone limitations section is present in the material read. Points a reader should weigh: IRT assumes a unidimensional latent ability and a monotone item response function, so a configuration that is strong on algebra and weak on geometry is compressed into one ability number — a known limitation of the psychometric model that the paper's own framing of specialized models makes salient. The difficulty parameter is estimated from the calibration matrix, so it is difficulty relative to the model pool, not an intrinsic property of the query; adding a much stronger model rescales it. And routing operates at the granularity of whole configurations chosen before generation, so it cannot revise the decision once reasoning reveals the problem to be harder than it looked.
method: An evaluation response matrix is collected by running each {reasoning model, reasoning budget} configuration on a calibration set of queries and recording correctness. That matrix is modelled with item response theory — the classical framework from educational assessment in which the probability that a respondent answers an item correctly is a function of the respondent's latent ability and the item's latent difficulty. Fitting the model yields one difficulty parameter per query and one ability parameter per configuration, on a shared scale, which is what makes the routing decision interpretable: a query is sent to the cheapest configuration whose estimated ability exceeds its estimated difficulty. To route queries never seen during calibration, difficulty is made a predictable function of the query rather than a free per-item parameter. To add a new model cheaply, its ability is estimated from a small adaptively chosen subset of calibration queries rather than the full set. Evaluation covers eight reasoning benchmarks spanning math, science and coding, against state-of-the-art routing baselines, with a separate out-of-distribution protocol.
one_liner: Routes each query to a {model, reasoning budget} configuration by fitting an item response theory model over an evaluation matrix, yielding interpretable query difficulties and configuration abilities, and sending harder queries to higher-ability configurations.
problem: Deploying reasoning models involves a performance-cost trade-off at two levels simultaneously — model size and reasoning budget — and both larger models and higher budgets cost more latency and money for better accuracy. With thousands of reasoning models available and providers exposing low/medium/high budget settings, choosing one configuration for all queries is wasteful on easy queries and inadequate on hard ones. Existing routing methods do not expose why a query was routed where, and adding a new model normally requires re-evaluating it on everything.

relevance.test-time-scaling: The external counterpart to the archive's internal difficulty estimator, and the one that will read most naturally to a statistics group. Where the reasoning-strength work reads a difficulty estimate the model already computed in its activations, this estimates difficulty as a latent parameter from an evaluation response matrix using item response theory — the same machinery used for standardized testing, with the same interpretability guarantee. That gives this topic two difficulty signals with complementary properties: one requires activation access and works per-query before generation, the other requires a calibration matrix and works for any model including closed ones. It also broadens what allocation means. Every other allocation method in this archive varies the budget for a fixed model; RADAR varies model *and* budget jointly, which is the decision an actual deployment faces. The IRT framing also supplies something the archive's difficulty discussions have lacked — a stated measurement model, with assumptions one can check, rather than a heuristic proxy.

results: RADAR outperforms state-of-the-art model routing methods across the eight benchmarks, and retains strong performance on out-of-distribution queries on all of them, including long-context document QA which is structurally unlike the math and science calibration data. The scalability claim is demonstrated by integrating additional models through a small dynamically selected query set rather than full re-evaluation. Because the fitted parameters are interpretable, the routing decisions are auditable — one can read off which queries the system considers hard and which configurations it considers capable, rather than only observing the routing outcome.
